newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council agrees on Zaire multinational force.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council agrees on Zaire multinational force.

text.p: The Security Council agreed during private consultations on Friday on a resolution to deploy a Canadian-led multinational force to help refugees in eastern Zaire and it would be adopted later in the day, British U.N. envoy Sir John Weston said.

"We have just agreed the resolution authorising the creation and deployment of the multinational force for eastern Zaire and we shall adopt it at 4 o'clock (2100 GMT) this afternoon," he told reporters.

"That's a very healthy outcome at the end of a few days of intensive work and we hope that the existence of this force, and if necessary the use of this force, will make all the difference in saving a large number of lives," Weston added.
He said he expected a unanimous vote, and that there had been only minor changes to the text of the resolution first circulated to council members Thursday night.

The multinational force, expected eventually to number some 10,000 troops, is to use "all necessary means" to get food, water and medical supplies to more than a million Rwandan Hutu refugees whose aid has been cut by fighting in the region.
The refugees fled to eastern Zaire in 1994 after the massacre in Rwanda of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Hutu troops and militia involved in the slaughter controlled most of the refugee camps, preventing the repatriation of those wishing to return home. But the camps were disrupted by recent fighting between Zairean Tutsis, backed by Rwanda, and the Zairean army.

Asked whether there was any concern Rwanda might not be willing to assist now that hundreds of thousands of the refugees were trekking home and Rwanda had said the force was unnecessary, Weston said the latest reports from Britain's ambassador in Kigali who had been in touch with Rwanda's vice president, "were very encouraging."

Earlier, Rwanda's U.N. envoy and its ambassador to Washington said the mandate of the planned force, to be headed by Canadian Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, was now irrelevant and resources should be made available instead to help resettle the refugees inside Rwanda.
United Nations spokeswoman Sylvana Foa expressed delight that huge numbers of Rwandan refugees were streaming home but insisted a multinational force was still badly needed.
She said the Geneva-based U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees had called the exodus the "largest and fastest homeward movement of refugees in history."

"Everybody is absolutely elated but we still desperately need the multinational force," she said. "We have stocks in Rwanda for about 450,000 people but we are going to need a lot of help to move these people around." Only a military operation could provide the required logistics, she added.

Rwanda's U.N. envoy, Gideon Kayianamura, said he was happy the refugees were returning but had asked the Security Council president and others involved "to rethink the mandate and the relevance of this multinational force in the circumstances."
"The much talked-about humanitarian tragedy of Rwandan refugees is now coming to an end. We need support to rehabilitate them inside the country," he said.
This was echoed by Rwanda's U.S. Ambassador Theogene Rudasingwa who told the same news conference: "The intervention is not relevant today."

He added: "The Rwandan government is insisting that whatever resources are available, including the tremendous resources that would have gone into supporting this multinational intervention, should be available in Rwanda so that we use them in a process that is definitely likely to be difficult in resettling the people in Rwanda."
The resolution to be adopted by the council calls for a four-month operation. It expresses the intention of establishing a follow-on U.N. operation to take over from the multinational force.

In a letter to Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali outlining the operation, Canadian U.N. envoy Robert Fowler said it would act under Chapter VII of the U.N. Charter, which authorises the use of force. But he stressed it was "not intended to interfere with the balance of military forces in the area nor to support the re-establishment of camps in which armed elements are able to operate."
